case_against: Federal school money comes with rules for a reason: it is meant to reach poor children, students with disabilities and others who might otherwise be overlooked. Turning it into no-strings block grants removes that guarantee. History shows block grants tend to shrink over time. When Congress folded 37 education programs into a block grant in 1981, overall funding for the combined programs was cut.

harms.what: Without targeting rules, money meant for the poorest districts could be spread to wealthier ones.

harms.who: Students with disabilities and English learners
harms.what: Programs written for their needs could lose dedicated funding once money is pooled.

history.what: Congress combined 75 grant programs, including 37 education programs, into nine block grants. Overall funding for the programs bundled together was cut 12%, about $1 billion.
history.lesson: Block grants have been used to cut spending. CRS also cites studies finding block grants' inflation-adjusted funding fell over time.

case_against: The U.S. already tried running student loans through private banks. Under the old guaranteed loan program, banks made the loans, but the government paid them extra subsidies to take part and repaid them when borrowers defaulted. Taxpayers carried most of the risk. Congress ended that program in 2010. Going back would bring in a middleman without lowering the risk to taxpayers.

harms.what: The government would again pay lenders subsidies and cover their losses on defaults.
Borrowers would deal with many private lenders again, adding complexity to a system already hard to navigate.

history.what: From 1994 to 2010, guaranteed private loans and direct federal loans ran side by side. In the guaranteed program, lenders received special allowance payments and were repaid by the government when loans defaulted. Congress ended new guaranteed loans as of July 1, 2010.
history.lesson: The government bore the risk under both systems, but the guaranteed system added extra payments to private lenders.

case_against: Closing the Education Department scatters school and college programs across agencies that were not built to run them. The department is already being taken apart without a law from Congress. About a third of staff were laid off in 2025, and 20 states sued, saying federal law requires the department to run its own programs. GAO found the department spent up to $38 million on months of paid leave for civil rights staff it later brought back.

harms.what: Programs moved to Labor, HHS and other agencies may face delays and confusion, and expertise is lost as staff leave.
States say the transfers upend decades of work on programs like career and technical education.
GAO found up to $38 million was spent on paid leave for civil rights employees before they were reinstated.

case_against: Title I sends about $18.4 billion a year to schools with many low-income children. Turning it into a no-strings block grant would remove the rules that make sure the money reaches those schools. Block grants have often lost value over time. Moving Title I out of the Education Department has already drawn a lawsuit from 20 states, which argue the law does not allow it.

harms.what: Without targeting rules, Title I money could be spread to schools with fewer poor children.
Districts that depend most on Title I could see their share shrink if the block grant loses value, as other block grants have.

case_against: Ending federal Title I money would pull about $18.4 billion a year from schools that serve low-income children. Title I's formulas are based on counts of children in poverty, so more help goes where more poor children live. Asking every state to replace that money on its own means poorer states would struggle most to fill the gap.

harms.what: Schools could lose staff, tutoring and other services now paid for with Title I money.
States with less tax base would have the hardest time replacing federal money.

case_against: The special education law exists because states once left children with disabilities out. When Congress passed it in 1975, it found that 1 million children with disabilities were shut out of public schools entirely. A no-strings block grant run by a health agency would weaken the rights and rules that changed that. Disability groups warn that moving special education to HHS treats it as a medical issue instead of an education right.

harms.what: Advocates such as The Arc warn students would be more likely to be segregated or treated as separate from their school community.
Rights to a free appropriate public education and to challenge schools could weaken if federal rules are removed.

history.what: Congress passed the Education for All Handicapped Children Act, now called IDEA, after finding that more than half of children with disabilities were not getting a proper education and 1 million were excluded from public schools.
history.lesson: Federal rules were added because states, left on their own, often failed these children. Removing those rules risks going backward.

case_against: Federal student aid is a huge, complicated system, and a hasty move risks mistakes that land on borrowers. About 7.8 million borrowers, owing $179 billion, are in default, and Treasury's debt collection office would have to take on all of them. CRS notes critics argue Treasury lacks expertise in student loans and may not be staffed for the job. GAO has agreed to look into the transfer.

harms.what: Millions could face collection by an office new to student loans, with risk of errors and lost relief options.
Later phases would move FAFSA support too, risking disruption in getting aid for college.

case_against: The Office for Civil Rights usually fixes problems by reaching agreements with schools; cutting off funds or going to court is rare. Limiting enforcement to court cases would make help slower, costlier and rarer for students facing discrimination. The Supreme Court ruled in 2001 that private people cannot sue to enforce Title VI's disparate impact rules, so cutting back agency enforcement leaves some kinds of discrimination with no one to enforce against it.

harms.what: Families would have fewer ways to get quick fixes, such as a school agreement to change a policy.

harms.who: Students harmed by unfair but neutral-sounding policies
harms.what: Private lawsuits over disparate impact are barred, so if the agency steps back, no one may enforce these rules.

case_against: These rules help borrowers who were cheated by their colleges, whose schools closed mid-program, or who spent 10 years in public service. Rolling them back puts the cost of a college's misconduct or collapse on students. Public Service Loan Forgiveness alone had helped about 1.25 million borrowers, totaling $93.4 billion, through April 2026. Two federal courts struck down the 2025 rule that narrowed it, finding it went beyond the law.

harms.what: Delaying the 2022 borrower defense rule brings back older, harder rules for getting loans canceled.
The older closed-school rules give less automatic relief to students left with debt and no degree.
Nurses, teachers and others at nonprofits or government jobs could lose credit toward forgiveness if their employer is disqualified.

case_against: The 2020 rule narrowed what counts as sexual harassment to conduct that is severe, pervasive and objectively offensive, a higher bar that can leave students without help until harassment becomes extreme. Defining sex only as sex at birth also strips transgender students of federal protection. Before this change, two federal appeals courts had ruled that barring transgender students from the bathroom that matches their gender identity can violate Title IX.

harms.what: Schools must act only once harassment meets a high bar, so some students may not get help early.
They lose federal recourse when schools exclude them from facilities or activities.

case_against: Writing a sex-at-birth definition into Title IX would permanently remove transgender students from the law's protection, ending an issue courts were still deciding. Two federal appeals courts had found that Title IX can protect transgender students from exclusion at school, while another disagreed. A law passed by Congress would close that question for every school in the country, no matter the facts of a student's case.

harms.what: They would have no Title IX claim when excluded or treated differently because they are transgender.

case_against: Dropping gender identity from the meaning of sex across the whole government leaves transgender students and workers without a federal place to turn when they face discrimination. Federal appeals courts in two circuits had ruled that Title IX can protect transgender students. Courts have been split on the question, but this policy ends federal help for these students everywhere at once.

harms.what: Federal agencies no longer investigate complaints that they were treated unfairly because of their gender identity.
Schools face mixed signals as federal policy, state laws and court rulings point in different directions.

case_against: Disparate impact rules catch policies that look neutral but fall much harder on one group without a good reason, such as school discipline rules. The Supreme Court ruled in 2001 that private people cannot sue to enforce these rules, so federal agencies are the only ones who can. If agencies stop investigating them, these kinds of unfair policies go unchecked.

harms.what: A neutral-sounding discipline policy that falls much harder on one race could no longer be challenged under these rules.
With private lawsuits already barred, they would have nowhere to take this type of claim.

case_against: Writing a rule that Title VI has no disparate impact standard erases protections agencies have used against policies that unfairly harm one race. Because the Supreme Court bars private lawsuits under these rules, removing them ends enforcement completely. Both the Justice and Education departments made the change without taking public comment.

harms.what: Policies in schools and other federally funded programs that fall much harder on one race without good reason could no longer be challenged on that basis.

case_against: Income-driven plans keep payments affordable for borrowers with low earnings. The new Repayment Assistance Plan replaces several of them and charges a $10 monthly minimum, while older plans could set a payment of zero for borrowers below a poverty-based cutoff. CRS calls the new plan considerably different from existing ones. Delinquencies have already jumped since payments resumed, and higher minimums could push more borrowers into default.

harms.what: Borrowers whose income is near or below the poverty line now owe at least $10 a month under the new plan.
CRS reports the share of borrowers 31-270 days delinquent rose from 0% to 16% in one quarter after relief ended.

case_against: The payment pause and forgiveness programs were relief that Congress and past administrations created for people in hard times. Ending them abruptly has real costs. CRS reports that after relief ended, the share of borrowers 31 to 270 days late jumped from 0% to 16% in one quarter, and defaults rose after that. Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which this item calls abuse, is a program Congress wrote into law in 2007.

harms.who: Borrowers who were on the SAVE plan
harms.what: Millions who had been in a payment pause were told to pick a new plan after the agreement to end SAVE.
Loans more than 90 days late are reported to credit bureaus, and loans become defaulted after 270 days of missed payments.

case_against: A single loan program with no interest subsidies and no forgiveness would make college costlier for the students with the least money. Subsidized loans spare low-income undergraduates from interest while in school. Removing forgiveness means borrowers with low earnings could pay for decades without ever clearing their debt. Even the 2025 law kept subsidized loans and forgiveness after 30 years, which shows how far this goes.

harms.what: They would pay interest while in school if subsidized loans ended.
Without any forgiveness, some could keep paying for decades without clearing their debt.

case_against: Letting states opt out of federal K-12 programs and spend the money on any lawful education purpose removes the rules that send help to poor children, English learners and other groups. It also weakens the reporting that shows whether those students are learning. Past block grants show that once money is pooled without targets, its value tends to shrink over time.

harms.what: Money meant for them could be spent on other priorities.
Without federal reporting rules, it is harder to see whether struggling groups of students are falling behind.

case_against: Grad PLUS and Parent PLUS loans help students pay for programs when other federal loans run out. Ending Grad PLUS, as the 2025 law did for new borrowers, leaves graduate students with new lifetime limits of $100,000, or $200,000 for professional programs. Students in costly fields like medicine may have to turn to private loans, which lack federal protections such as income-driven repayment and Public Service Loan Forgiveness.

harms.what: Those whose costs exceed the new limits must find other money, often private loans.
Parent PLUS is now capped at $20,000 a year and $65,000 per student, which may not cover costs at some schools.

case_against: Public Service Loan Forgiveness rewards people who spend 10 years in public service jobs, like teaching, law enforcement and work at nonprofits. Congress created it in 2007 to draw people into these jobs. Through April 2026, about 1.25 million borrowers had received forgiveness totaling $93.4 billion. Ending it would break a promise to workers who took lower-paying jobs counting on it.

harms.who: Teachers, police, nonprofit staff and other public workers
harms.what: They would lose forgiveness they planned their careers around.
They could find it harder to hire and keep workers without this benefit.

case_against: The Education Secretary's power to change loan terms has been used in emergencies. In March 2020, as COVID-19 hit, the department set interest to 0% and let borrowers pause payments, and Congress then wrote a pause into law. Stripping this power would leave borrowers waiting on Congress during the next crisis. The Supreme Court already limited broad cancellation in 2023, so the change is not needed to stop that.

harms.what: Quick relief like the March 2020 payment pause could be delayed or blocked.

case_against: Indirect costs pay for the labs, safety systems and support staff that research needs but that cannot be tied to one project. Rates are negotiated and range from 30% to 70%. Capping them low would shift costs to universities, and CRS notes the hit could fall hardest on public and smaller universities without big endowments. When NIH tried a 15% cap in 2025, a federal court blocked it and an appeals court agreed.

harms.what: They have less private support to cover research costs the government would no longer pay.
Less research capacity could slow medical and scientific discoveries that federal grants pay for.

case_against: Competitive grants pay for targeted work like training new teachers. In 2025 the department canceled 104 of 109 grants in two teacher-training programs, about $600 million. A 10% cut to large formula grants would also hit Title I and special education, which serve low-income students and students with disabilities. Congress rejected these cuts in 2026 and raised both programs slightly.

harms.what: Most grants in two teacher-training programs were canceled in 2025.

harms.what: A 10% cut to Title I and special education grants would reduce services for them.
